text:
In the autumn when the university began referring to its students as residents, Mira received three notices concerning a stain above her bed. The first asked for its dimensions. The second explained how to measure it. The third informed her that her case had been closed.

“It’s shaped like Denmark,” Lizzy said, standing on the mattress.

“Is that useful?”

“Probably not to Denmark.”

Their room occupied a converted hospital. The university called it an experimental residential community. Grooves remained where trolleys had struck the corridor walls. A fern stood in the old admissions window, receiving everyone who came home.

Mira studied social history, though she mostly corrected transcripts for a professor writing about the disappearance of skilled labor. Her mother, who cleaned holiday cottages, called this typing. Mira had tried explaining the distinction and heard herself becoming unbearable.

Her boyfriend, Carl, lived across the courtyard, where the windows opened fully.

***

Carl played the cello. His father conducted an orchestra; his mother bought him shirts and apologized for buying them. He made coffee in an apparatus requiring more attention than Mira liked to receive in the morning.

He was generous. He paid before she could refuse, then forgot he had paid. This was precisely what she resented.

One Thursday, he bought recital tickets without consulting her.

“I’m working.”

“You can swap.”

“It isn’t a shift.”

“You know what I mean.”

She did know. That was part of the difficulty.

***

Martin organized the meeting about residential conditions. He was a doctoral student with a beard that probably made him look younger than his shaved face would have. Seven people attended.

“Encouraging,” he said.

Mira had come because of the ceiling.

On a whiteboard he had written RENT / CARE / BELONGING. The third word embarrassed her, though explaining why would have revealed that she wanted it.

Afterward, he asked her to gather accounts from students. He had read her essay about workhouse laundries.

“You make structures visible through ordinary life.”

She carried the sentence home like something breakable.

Lizzy was eating cereal from a saucepan.

“Careful,” she said. “That’s how they recruit you.”

“Who?”

“Men who own whiteboard pens.”

They collected statements at the kitchen table: broken locks, mold, disciplinary warnings. One student had been charged for a chair he said had never existed.

Martin wanted a public report.

“Something that can move.”

Leaning over Mira’s laptop, he made her conscious of her neck. Carl had kissed her there that morning, and she had shrugged him away.

***

At the university archive, Johan helped Mira find the hospital plans. He was a Swedish engineering student who considered questions before answering.

“Are you translating?” she asked.

“Usually I am deciding whether I know.”

The plans showed a washroom above her bedroom.

“So Denmark might be sewage.”

“Old sewage, possibly.”

He inspected the stain, photographed a pipe joint, and contacted maintenance. Three days later, a plumber arrived.

Over coffee, Mira told him she sometimes dreamed she had moved home and was pretending to her mother that she was only visiting.

“Would that be so bad?”

She had intended the story to be funny.

“I don’t know.”

He left her answer uncorrected.

***

In November, Lizzy asked to borrow four hundred pounds. They were beside the supermarket’s reduced vegetables.

Mira said she did not have it. She had four hundred and sixty-eight; her scholarship installment was six weeks away.

“My father’s decided I’m learning independence,” Lizzy said.

He had stopped paying her rent after discovering that a woman he believed was her tutor had been her girlfriend. Now the woman was neither, but still had Lizzy’s winter coat.

“Don’t put that in your thing.”

“What thing?”

“The suffering document.”

“Of course not.”

That evening, Mira transferred two hundred pounds.

When she told Carl, he said, “You should be careful.”

“She’ll pay it back.”

“I didn’t say she wouldn’t.”

But he had made the loan look like evidence.

Their quarrel moved through money, Martin, and a visit to Carl’s parents.

“You make it impossible to do anything nice for you.”

She could have said accepting things frightened her. Instead she asked whether nice was his highest ambition.

“That was shitty,” he said.

At home, Lizzy had washed every dish except the saucepan.

***

The report needed someone whose circumstances showed how several pressures converged. One student withdrew permission; another stopped answering messages.

At midnight, Mira wrote about a student whose family had withdrawn support after the disclosure of a same-sex relationship. She changed the amount owed and called the student A.

She told herself she had preserved the truth while removing the person.

“This is the piece,” Martin said.

She considered explaining. Then he began discussing the introduction, and the moment became harder to recover.

The report appeared on Monday. By noon, a local journalist had shared it.

At three, Lizzy called.

“Take it down.”

“It’s anonymous.”

In the silence, Mira heard what she had said.

“My father’s not an idiot.”

“I changed things.”

“You promised.”

“I know.”

“What did you think?”

She had thought of Martin reading it. Of forcing the university to answer. Of herself as useful.

Lizzy hung up.

Martin said removing the report would undermine the work. Mira deleted it from their website. He uploaded it elsewhere.

“You can’t give one person a veto over a collective project,” he told her outside the library.

“She didn’t agree to be in it.”

“We protected her identity.”

“Not from people who know her.”

He rubbed his forehead.

“You wrote it, Mira.”

“Yes.”

She had wanted him to say something that would let her hate him cleanly. Instead he had said what she needed to remember.

***

Lizzy stayed with a friend for nine days.

Mira apologized, removed every copy she could reach, and contacted the journalist. She told the other contributors exactly how their accounts had been used. Two withdrew. One corrected his name; he had wanted it included.

Martin stopped copying her into messages.

Carl arrived with groceries. Mira cried while clearing space on the table.

“I’m not the injured person.”

“I know.”

They cooked expensive mushrooms badly. He mentioned an orchestra audition in another city.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I didn’t want you to think I assumed you’d come.”

She had treated his certainty as the chief fact of his character. Now she saw the effort of keeping it supplied.

They broke up on Sunday, each trying unsuccessfully to make it easier for the other.

***

At the archive, Johan asked whether Mira was ill.

“Just discredited.”

“Officially?”

“Among people I know.”

“Less organized. Maybe worse.”

She told him what she had done.

“Why didn’t you ask her?”

“Because she would have said no.”

Around them stood boxes of records restricted by their donors: not to be opened, quoted, photographed without permission. Mira had observed those conditions solemnly. A dead administrator’s correspondence had received more respect than Lizzy’s living request.

Johan closed the box.

“Do you want to go outside?”

They walked beside the canal. She wanted to kiss him and distrusted how welcome the wish felt.

“I’m not very good company.”

“I noticed.”

He was smiling.

***

Lizzy returned with two bags and a borrowed plant.

Mira stood beside her bed.

“You don’t need to look like you’re waiting for a sentence,” Lizzy said.

They became polite. They asked before borrowing milk, announced visitors. Mira discovered how much friendship consisted of permissions granted so long ago that everyone had forgotten the granting.

One night, Lizzy asked her to read an application for emergency housing support.

“Only grammar.”

“Only grammar.”

Mira corrected a comma and changed “effect” to “affect.”

“Is that all?”

“Yes.”

Lizzy clicked submit.

In February, the housing office held a consultation. Martin chaired the student delegation. Mira sat near the back.

A first-year student asked who was responsible if someone entered her room through its broken lock. The director spoke without identifying anyone.

Afterward, Mira offered the maintenance supervisor’s name and help writing an email.

“I can manage,” the student said.

Johan left in March. By then they had slept together and argued about whether his refusal to plan was reasonable or convenient.

At the station, he returned a borrowed book with a receipt inside. He had spilled coffee on the original and bought a replacement.

“You could have told me.”

“I am telling you.”

They agreed to visit in June, which seemed insufficient and worth arranging.

That evening, Mira worked beneath the repaired ceiling. Fresh paint left an irregular patch brighter than its surroundings.

Her mother called to ask if she was eating properly. Mira described the dinner she intended to cook as though it had happened.

Afterward, she put water on for pasta and took two bowls from the cupboard.

She messaged Lizzy: Would she be home?

Not for ages. Eat without me.

Mira put one bowl back.
